draft.title: Counter-narratives
card: A dominant narrative is the version of events a culture tells most often and treats as the normal one. It usually favours the views of those with the most power.
A counter-narrative tells the story from a perspective the dominant story left out or silenced. It can come from a character, group or community whose experience was ignored.
It challenges who is seen as the hero and whose experience counts. A figure shown as a villain or a background extra may become the narrator.
A counter-narrative does not just add a new view. It asks readers to question the dominant story and what it left unsaid.
draft.remember: A counter-narrative gives voice to those the dominant story left out, and challenges that story.

opts: Tells a story from a perspective the dominant story left out
Repeats the dominant story in a shorter and simpler form
Updates the setting of a story for a modern audience
Gives the dominant story's hero a longer speaking part
a.why: A counter-narrative brings in a viewpoint that was missing and so challenges the dominant story. Simply repeating or updating a story does not question whose experience counts.
a.clue: Think about whose voice was missing.

b.q: A town's old legend tells how a settler heroically built a bridge. Ana writes a story told by a local worker who built it and was never named. Why is this a counter-narrative?
opts: It challenges who is seen as the hero and whose work counts
It uses the same hero but sets the story in a new year
It retells the legend in order to praise the settler more
It shortens the legend so that it is easier to remember
b.why: The unnamed worker's view was left out of the legend, and the new story questions who deserves credit. Changing only the date or praising the settler would keep the dominant story as it was.
b.clue: Ask whose experience the legend left out.

a.best: Tells a story from a perspective the dominant story left out

b.best: It challenges who is seen as the hero and whose work counts
